tpl:g10m14s3-1-1:neither-region:
judge: solution_ok is False — The mathematics is correct in all three instances, and I re-derived each key independently. g001 (1 to 38, multiples of 6 and 5): n(A)=6, n(B)=7, overlap {30}, union 12, answer 26. g002 (1 to 30, multiples of 7 and 4): n(A)=4, n(B)=7, overlap {28}, union 10, answer 20. g004 (1 to 49, multiples of 5 and 6): n(A)=9, n(B)=8, overlap {30}, union 16, answer 33. Every set listing, count and subtraction checks out. The method is the book's: fill the overlap first, take away-only counts, add up the circles, subtract from n(S). The stems are unambiguous and self-contained. The family has no options, so there are no distractors to judge, and the numeric key is the count the stem asks for.

I set solution_ok to false for one reason, a template defect in step 4 of every instance. It reads "That is $1$ numbers", which should be "1 number". The overlap is exactly 1 in all three instances, so every student who opens the worked solution sees the error. Fix: pluralise from the overlap count, or word it without a count ("the overlap holds ...").

Not blocking, but worth knowing: the overlap is always exactly 1 (lcm 30 or 28 in a range under 60). That is fine for the "neither region" skill, but it makes the family narrow and is why the glitch shows every time.
tpl:g10m14s7-1-2:pairs-count:
judge: solution_ok is False — The keys are all correct, but solution step 5 has a wording defect in g003 and g010, so I am rejecting on solution_ok.

I recomputed each instance by hand.
- g001: A∩B = {1}, so (i) is not exclusive. A∪B = {1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10}, so A'∩B' = {6,11}, so (ii) is not exclusive. (iii) is always exclusive. The count is 1, matching the key.
- g003: A = {1,4,5,6,9} and B = {2,3,7,8,10} are disjoint and together cover S = 1..10. So (i) is exclusive, A'∩B' is empty so (ii) is exclusive, and (iii) is exclusive. The count is 3, matching the key.
- g010: A = {2,3,4,7,9} and B = {1,5,6,8,10} are disjoint and together cover S = 1..10. The same reasoning gives 3, matching the key.

The step 2 to 4 checks in each solution are correct. There are no multiple-choice options (numeric answer), so distractors is empty and distractors_ok is vacuously true. The key is a bare whole number, which is the form the stem asks for. No answer_check was in the file, so I could not compare it with the key.

Defect: step 5 is a fixed sentence reused in every instance: "this pair is mutually exclusive, even though A and B may overlap." In g003 and g010, step 2 has just shown that A and B do not overlap, so the "even though" clause contradicts the worked solution. It is hedged with "may", so it is not strictly false, and I do not think it teaches a wrong fact. It is still confusing for a Grade 10 reader. The fix is to make the clause conditional: include it only when A∩B is non-empty, as in g001, and otherwise drop it or say that here (A∪B)' is empty.

Minor, non-blocking points on context:
- Pair (iii) is exclusive in every instance, so the question really tests (i) and (ii). That is acceptable for an advanced-tier conceptual item.
- In g003 and g010 the complement (A∪B)' is the empty event and A∪B = S. The solution never says so. This is mathematically fine, but a student may wonder whether an empty event counts. The solution could name it, for example "(A∪B)' = {}, the impossible event".

misconceptions.label: Divides by the outcomes outside the event instead of by all the outcomes
misconceptions.description: The student writes n(E) over the number of outcomes that are not in the event, comparing the event with the rest, instead of over n(S), the total number of outcomes in the sample space.

misconceptions.label: Counts the outcomes outside the event instead of inside it
misconceptions.description: The student counts the outcomes that do not belong to the event and writes that count over n(S), so n(E) is the wrong set.

misconceptions.label: Treats outcomes that are not equally likely as if they were
misconceptions.description: The student counts the kinds of result (for example the colours in a bag) as the outcomes and divides by that count, or applies n(E)/n(S) to a situation whose outcomes are not equally likely.

misconceptions.label: Reads only the part both circles share
misconceptions.description: The student lists only the elements that sit inside both circles, as if the event set were just the shared part rather than everything inside its own circle.

misconceptions.label: Reads the numbers outside the circle
misconceptions.description: The student lists the elements that lie outside the circle for the event, instead of the elements inside it.

misconceptions.label: Lists only the part of A that is outside B
misconceptions.description: The student reads $A\cup B$ as just the first set and writes down only the elements that are in $A$ but not in $B$, leaving out the overlap and everything in $B$.

misconceptions.label: Takes only the overlap as the union
misconceptions.description: The student writes down only the elements that are in both sets, the overlap of the two circles, as if $A\cup B$ meant "$A$ and $B$" instead of "$A$ or $B$".

misconceptions.label: Gives one whole event set instead of the shared elements
misconceptions.description: The student writes out every element of one event set ($A$ or $B$) and calls that the intersection, instead of keeping only the elements that are also in the other set.

misconceptions.label: Treats two possible results as events that can happen together
misconceptions.description: The student sees that each event is a real possibility in the same set-up (orange juice and apple juice are both in the fridge, red velvet and vanilla are both in the packet) and calls the events not mutually exclusive, instead of asking whether one single pick can be in both events.

misconceptions.label: Takes events described in different ways as having nothing in common
misconceptions.description: The student sees red and picture as two different kinds of description (a colour and a type of card), assumes a card cannot be both, and calls the events mutually exclusive without checking whether any card is in both event sets.

misconceptions.label: Thinks mutually exclusive events must cover every outcome
misconceptions.description: The student rejects two events as not mutually exclusive because some other outcome belongs to neither of them (a tie, a grape juice), as if mutually exclusive meant that the two events use up everything that can happen.

misconceptions.label: Lists numbers from inside the event instead of outside it
misconceptions.description: The student writes down numbers that lie inside the event's circle or circles (the event itself, or part of it) instead of the numbers of the sample space that are not in the event.

questions.stem: A box contains coloured blocks: 31 purple, 26 orange, 30 white and 27 pink. A block is selected at random. Which of the following is the probability that the block is purple?

canonical_solution.text_md: First we work out how many blocks there are in total. This gives us the sample space: $n(S)=31+26+30+27=114$ .
The event is that the block is purple. There are $31$ purple blocks, so $n(E)=31$ .
Every block is equally likely to be selected, so: $\begin{aligned}P(\text{purple})&=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}\\&=\frac{31}{114}\end{aligned}$ This fraction is already in simplest form.

The four colours are not equally likely, because there are different numbers of blocks of each colour, so the answer is not $\frac{1}{4}$ . The total $114$ counts all the blocks, not only the ones that are not purple, and the numerator counts the purple blocks, not the others.

questions.stem: Team 1 and Team 2 play 10 football matches against each other. Each match is one trial. The final scores, written as Team 1 – Team 2, in matches 1 to 10 were: 1–1, 1–1, 3–1, 0–3, 4–4, 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 1–1 and 4–1. What is the relative frequency of Team 1 not losing a match, that is, of Team 1 either winning or drawing? Give your answer as a decimal.

canonical_solution.text_md: Recall the formula for relative frequency: $f=\frac{p}{t}$, where $p$ is the number of positive trials (trials in which the event occurs) and $t$ is the total number of trials.
Each match is one trial, so the total number of trials is $t=10$. The event is that Team 1 does not lose, so a positive trial is a match that Team 1 wins or that ends in a draw.

For each match, subtract Team 2's goals from Team 1's goals. In matches 1 to 10 the differences are $ 0, 0, 2, -3, 0, -1, -2, -2, 0, 3 $. A positive difference is a win for Team 1, a difference of $0$ is a draw, and a negative difference is a loss for Team 1.
Count the positive trials: Team 1 won $ 2 $ matches and drew $ 4 $ matches, so $p=2+4=6$.
Calculate the relative frequency: $f=\frac{p}{t}=\frac{6}{10}=0.6$
Therefore, the relative frequency of Team 1 not losing a match is $0.6$.

questions.stem: Pieces of paper labelled with the numbers $1$ to $32$ are placed in a box and the box is shaken. One piece of paper is taken out and then replaced. The event $A$ is taking a piece of paper labelled with a factor of $32$. Write down the set $A$ and use it to find $n(A)$, the number of elements in $A$.

canonical_solution.text_md: The sample space $S$ is all the numbers that can be on the piece of paper: the whole numbers from $1$ to $32$, so $n(S) = 32$.
The event $A$ contains the numbers in $S$ that are factors of $32$, that is, the numbers that divide $32$ exactly with no remainder.
Checking the numbers from $1$ to $32$ one by one gives $A = \{1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 8,\ 16,\ 32\}$. Notice that $1$ and $32$ are both factors of $32$, so both belong in $A$.
Counting the elements of $A$ gives $n(A) = 6$.

questions.stem: A sample space $S$ has 20 equally likely outcomes, so $n(S)=20$. For two events $A$ and $B$, $n(A)=9$, $n(B)=7$ and $n(A\cap B)=3$. Calculate $P(A\cup B)$. Give your answer as a decimal number, rounded to two decimal places.

canonical_solution.text_md: Use the identity $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. Subtracting $P(A\cap B)$ stops the outcomes that lie in both events from being counted twice.
Find each probability using $P(X)=\frac{n(X)}{n(S)}$:
$\begin{aligned}P(A)&=\frac{9}{20}=0.45\\P(B)&=\frac{7}{20}=0.35\\P(A\cap B)&=\frac{3}{20}=0.15\end{aligned}$
Calculate $P(A\cup B)$:
$\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\\&=(0.45)+(0.35)-(0.15)\\&=0.65\end{aligned}$
Therefore, the value of $P(A\cup B)$ is $0.65$.

questions.stem: Fiona has $66$ labelled discs, which are numbered from $1$ to $66$. If a disc is selected at random, what is the probability that the disc number is a multiple of both $3$ and $9$? Give your answer as a decimal number, rounded to two decimal places.

canonical_solution.text_md: A disc that is a multiple of $3$ and of $9$ lies in both events. Let $A$ be the event 'a multiple of $3$' and $B$ the event 'a multiple of $9$'. We need $P(A\cap B)$.
Since $9=3\times3$, every multiple of $9$ is also a multiple of $3$.
So the set of discs that are multiples of both $3$ and $9$ is the same as the set of multiples of $9$: $9$, $18$, $27$, $\ldots$
The largest multiple of $9$ that is not more than $66$ is $7\times9=63$ (the next one, $72$, is more than $66$), so $n(A\cap B)=7$.
The sample space has $n(S)=66$ discs, so $P(A\cap B)=\frac{n(A\cap B)}{n(S)}=\frac{7}{66}$.
Rounded to two decimal places, $\frac{7}{66}\approx0.11$.
Therefore, the probability that the disc number is a multiple of both $3$ and $9$ is $0.11$.

$P(\text{pink})=\frac{3}{60}$ and $P(\text{black})=\frac{25}{60}$.
A sock cannot be both pink and black, so the events are mutually exclusive and $P(\text{pink or black})=P(\text{pink})+P(\text{black})$.
$P(\text{pink or black})=\frac{3}{60}+\frac{25}{60}=\frac{28}{60}=\frac{7}{15}$

questions.stem: A group of learners work with the sample space $S = \{n : n \in \mathbb{Z}, 4 \leq n \leq 18\}$. Two events in $S$ are $A = \{5, 7, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 18\}$ and $B = \{5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 14, 17\}$. They are asked to identify the complementary event set of $(A \cap B)$, also known as $(A \cap B)'$. Write down the elements of $(A \cap B)'$ in increasing order, separated by commas.

canonical_solution.text_md: The sample space $S$ contains every integer from $4$ to $18$, so it has 15 elements.
$A \cap B$ is the set of elements that are in both $A$ and $B$: $A \cap B = \{5, 7, 9, 10, 14\}$.

The complementary event set $(A \cap B)'$ is every element of $S$ that is not in $A \cap B$. That includes the elements of $S$ that are in only one of the two events, and the elements that are in neither event.
The elements of $S$ in $A$ only are $\{13, 16, 18\}$, the elements in $B$ only are $\{6, 11, 17\}$, and the elements in neither $A$ nor $B$ are $\{4, 8, 12, 15\}$.
Together these are every element of $S$ that is not in $A \cap B$, so $(A \cap B)' = \{4, 6, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18\}$.

They are asked to identify the complementary event set of $(A \cup B)$, also known as $(A \cup B)'$. Write down the elements of $(A \cup B)'$ in increasing order, separated by commas.

canonical_solution.text_md: $A \cup B$ is the set of elements that are in $A$, in $B$, or in both: $A \cup B = \{2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15\}$.
The complementary event set $(A \cup B)'$ is every element of the sample space that is not in $A \cup B$, that is, every element that is in neither $A$ nor $B$.
Checking each integer from 1 to 15 against $A \cup B$, the integers that are not in it are $\{1, 3, 7, 9, 12\}$, so $(A \cup B)' = \{1, 3, 7, 9, 12\}$.

questions.stem: A number is chosen from the sample space $S = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 12\}$. Event $A = \{ 2, 4, 6, 10 \}$. Which one of the following events is mutually exclusive with $A$?

canonical_solution.text_md: Two events are mutually exclusive when they cannot occur at the same time. This means that no outcome is in both events: their intersection is empty.
Event $A = \{ 2, 4, 6, 10 \}$. Check each option for an outcome that is also in $A$.
The option $\{ 1, 5, 10 \}$ has the outcome 10 in common with $A$. Both events occur if 10 is chosen, so they are not mutually exclusive.
The option $\{ 2, 3, 4 \}$ has the outcomes 2 and 4 in common with $A$, so they are not mutually exclusive.
The option $\{ 6, 8, 12 \}$ has the outcome 6 in common with $A$. Both events occur if 6 is chosen, so they are not mutually exclusive.
The option $\{ 7, 9, 11 \}$ has no outcome in common with $A$: none of 7, 9 and 11 is in $A$. So $A \cap \{ 7, 9, 11 \} = \varnothing$.
Because the intersection is empty, the two events can never occur at the same time. The event that is mutually exclusive with $A$ is $\{ 7, 9, 11 \}$.

questions.stem: A box contains coloured blocks: $30$ purple, $19$ orange, $10$ white and $13$ pink. A block is selected at random. What is the probability that the block is neither purple nor white? Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.

canonical_solution.text_md: Count all the blocks in the box: $30+19+10+13=72$ blocks.
A block that is neither purple nor white is the complement of a block that is purple or white. The number of purple or white blocks is $30+10=40$, so $P(\text{purple or white})=\frac{40}{72}$.
An event and its complement have probabilities that add up to $1$, so $P(\text{neither purple nor white})=1-P(\text{purple or white})=1-\frac{40}{72}=\frac{32}{72}$.
Check: the orange and pink blocks number $19+13=32$, which agrees. In simplest form, $P(\text{neither purple nor white})=\frac{4}{9}$.

questions.stem: A class has $28$ learners. $18$ of them play football and $13$ of them play hockey, and $5$ play neither football nor hockey. The numbers for football and for hockey each include the learners who play both. How many learners play both football and hockey?

canonical_solution.text_md: The $5$ learners who play neither lie outside both circles, so the other $28 - 5 = 23$ learners play football or hockey (or both): $n(F \text{ or } H) = 23$.
Use the identity $n(F \text{ or } H) = n(F) + n(H) - n(F \text{ and } H)$: $23 = 18 + 13 - n(F \text{ and } H)$.
So $n(F \text{ and } H) = 18 + 13 - 23 = 8$ learners play both.
